lessons.title: Making friends
lessons.scenario: Smarty meets Omar and Zara at the café and hears how they became friends.

items.example: I got to know somebody new at school.
items.note: Say 'get to know somebody' when you spend time with a person and learn about them.

items.example: We hang out at the café on Friday.
items.note: Use 'hang out' for spending relaxed free time together with friends.

items.example: I get on well with my cousin.
items.note: Say 'get on well with' someone when you are friendly and enjoy being together.

items.example: We have a lot in common because we both love music.
items.note: Use 'have a lot in common' when two people like the same hobbies or subjects.

items.example: We lost touch after we finished school.
items.note: Say 'lose touch' when you stop speaking or sending messages to an old friend.

items.example: I made friends with Zara in art class.
items.note: Use 'make friends with' someone when you become friends for the first time.

grammar.title: Talking about friendship in the past and present
grammar.explanation: Use the present form (get, hang, make, lose) for habits now, and the past form (got, hung, made, lost) to tell how you met.
examples: I made friends with Leo last year.
We hang out at the park every weekend.

practice.prompt: You become friends with a new student. Which phrase fits?
practice.explanation: Make friends with means to become friends with someone.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: We hang out at the café on Saturday.
practice.answer: We hang out at the café on Saturday.
options: We hang out at the café on Saturday.
We lose touch at the café on Saturday.
We go to school on Saturday.
practice.explanation: Hang out means to spend relaxed time together.

practice.prompt: Match the two halves of each sentence.

pairs.left: We like the same music, so we
I like Sam very much and I
We never text now, so we

practice.explanation: Match each situation to the friendship phrase with the right meaning.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence.
practice.answer: I got to know Omar at the library.
practice.explanation: Got to know is the past form of get to know.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence.
practice.text: Mia and Ana ___ because they both play tennis.
practice.explanation: When two friends enjoy the same sport, they have a lot in common.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud.
practice.text: I get on well with my new friend.
practice.answer: I get on well with my new friend.
practice.explanation: Get on well with means to have a good, friendly relationship.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence about the past.
practice.text: I ___ Ben last year and we became good friends.
practice.explanation: Last year is in the past, so use met.

story.hook: How did Omar and Zara become best friends?

image.describe: Smarty the black cat sitting at a cozy wooden café table with two friendly cat friends, Omar and Zara, drinking tea and smiling.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Hello, Omar and Zara! How did you two meet?

lines.speaker: Omar
lines.text: Zara was only an acquaintance at first, but I got to know her in science class.

lines.speaker: Zara
lines.text: Omar is very cheerful, so I made friends with him quickly.

lines.speaker: Omar
lines.text: We found out we have a lot in common, like hiking and music.

lines.speaker: Zara
lines.text: We get on well with each other and we hang out here to chat every week.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: I hope you never lose touch!

questions.prompt: Where did Omar get to know Zara?
questions.explanation: Omar says he got to know her in science class.

questions.prompt: Why do Omar and Zara have a lot in common?
questions.explanation: Omar says they have a lot in common, like hiking and music.

mission.setup: You are at the café with Smarty. Tell Smarty about a friend you know.

turns.smarty: How did you make friends with your best friend?
accept: ^i (?:made friends with|got to know|met) (?:him|her|my friend|sam|mia|leo|ana) at (?:school|the park|the cafe|work)$
^we (?:met|got to know each other) at (?:school|the park|the cafe|work)$
turns.example: I made friends with Mia at school.
turns.hint: Say where you met or made friends with your friend.

turns.smarty: That is nice! Do you get on well with your friend?
accept: ^yes i get on well with (?:him|her|my friend)$
^yes we (?:get on well|hang out|have a lot in common)$
turns.example: Yes, I get on well with her.
turns.hint: Say Yes, I get on well with him or her.

exposure.gloss: someone you know a little, not a close friend
happy and smiling
talk in a friendly, relaxed way

lessons.title: Been there
lessons.scenario: Mia and Sam show Smarty travel photos at the café.

items.example: I have been to France and Spain.
items.note: Say 'I have been to' a place when you visited it at some time in your life.

items.example: I have never tried Japanese soup.
items.note: Use 'I have never tried' for a food, sport, or activity you have not done in your life.

items.example: I have visited three countries so far.
items.note: Add 'so far' to mean up to now, with more still possible in the future.

items.example: We have not seen Sam for ages.
items.note: Say 'for ages' when you mean for a very long time.

items.example: I have played tennis once or twice.
items.note: Use 'once or twice' when you have done something only one or two times.

items.example: Have you ever been to Italy?
items.note: Put 'ever' in questions to ask about any time in a person's whole life.

grammar.title: Present perfect for life experiences
grammar.explanation: Use have or has + past participle (been, tried, visited) to talk about experiences in your life without saying the exact date.
examples: I have been to Japan once or twice.
Have you ever tried spicy noodles?

practice.prompt: You visited Germany in the past and came back. Which phrase fits?
practice.explanation: I have been to means you visited a place at some time in your life.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: I have never tried tennis.
practice.explanation: Never tried means you have not done it at any time in your life.

practice.prompt: Match each phrase with its meaning.
practice.explanation: Each expression describes how much or how long up to now.

practice.prompt: Build the question.
practice.answer: Have you ever been to Uzbekistan?
practice.explanation: Use Have you ever been to to ask about a place someone has visited.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence.
practice.text: We have read two books ___ this month.
practice.explanation: So far means up to now in this month.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud.
practice.text: I have been to Japan once or twice.
practice.answer: I have been to Japan once or twice.
practice.explanation: Once or twice tells how many times you visited.

practice.prompt: Complete the question.
practice.text: ___ tried spicy fish soup?
practice.explanation: Use Have you ever with tried to ask about life experience.

story.hook: Which unusual activity has Sam never tried?

image.describe: Smarty the black cat looking at travel postcards spread on a café table with Mia and Sam.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: Look at this keepsake from my trip! I have been to Italy and Spain so far.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Fantastic! Have you ever been to a desert, Sam?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Yes, I have been to a desert once or twice with my uncle.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: I have never tried riding a camel. It looks unusual!

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: I have wanted to go back there for ages.

questions.prompt: How many times has Sam been to a desert?
questions.explanation: Sam says he has been to a desert once or twice.

questions.prompt: Which countries has Mia been to so far?
questions.explanation: Mia says she has been to Italy and Spain so far.

mission.setup: Smarty asks you about places you have visited and things you have tried.

turns.smarty: Have you ever been to another country?
accept: ^(?:yes )?i have been to (?:uzbekistan|england|brazil|france|germany|spain|italy|china|japan)(?: once or twice)?$
turns.example: I have been to England once or twice.
turns.hint: Say I have been to... and name a country.

turns.smarty: What is something you have never tried?
accept: ^i have never tried (?:sushi|tennis|climbing|spicy soup|japanese food|italian food|french bread)$
turns.example: I have never tried spicy soup.
turns.hint: Start with I have never tried...

exposure.gloss: a small object you keep to remember a place or person
different from what you normally see
wonderful and very exciting

lessons.title: How long?
lessons.scenario: Ben and Lily tell Smarty how long they have lived in town and played music.

items.example: How long have you known Lily?
items.note: Ask 'How long have you…?' to find out the time from the start until now.

items.example: I have studied English for three years.
items.note: Use 'for' with a number of minutes, days, months, or years to show how long.

items.example: I have played the piano since I was a child.
items.note: Use 'since' with a starting point in the past, like a year, a day, or 'since I was a child'.

items.example: I have lived in this house all my life.
items.note: Say 'all my life' for something that started when you were a baby and is still true.

items.example: Have you visited the museum recently?
items.note: Use 'recently' for something that happened a short time ago.

items.example: I have been very busy at school lately.
items.note: Put 'lately' at the end of a sentence to talk about the past few days or weeks.

grammar.title: for vs. since with the present perfect
grammar.explanation: Use for + a length of time (for three years, for ages). Use since + when it started (since Monday, since I was a child).
examples: We have been friends for three years.
She has lived here since she was a child.

practice.prompt: Which phrase gives a starting point in the past?
practice.explanation: Since shows when an action or state began.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence with the right time phrase.
practice.text: Ben has played the guitar ___.
practice.explanation: Use for with a period of time like three years.

practice.prompt: Match each question or start with the best ending.
practice.explanation: Match the grammar structure and meaning of each time expression.

practice.prompt: Build the question.
practice.answer: How long have you studied music?
practice.explanation: Start with How long have you to ask about duration up to now.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: I have started painting recently.
options: I have painted all my life.
practice.explanation: Recently means a short time ago.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud.
practice.text: I have lived here all my life.
practice.answer: I have lived here all my life.
practice.explanation: All my life means from birth until now.

practice.prompt: Smarty has known Ben for a very long time. Which phrase fits?
practice.explanation: For ages means for a very long time.

story.hook: How long has Lily played the violin?

image.describe: Smarty the black cat talking with Ben and Lily outside a sunny café, with Lily holding a violin case.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: How long have you lived in this neighbourhood, Ben?

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: I have lived here all my life! My family has been here for a decade.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: And what about you, Lily? How long have you played the violin?

lines.speaker: Lily
lines.text: I have played since I was a child. Music was my childhood dream.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: We have practised together for three years, and we have written a new song recently.

lines.speaker: Lily
lines.text: Yes, we have worked very hard lately!

questions.prompt: How long has Ben lived in the neighbourhood?
questions.explanation: Ben says he has lived there all his life.

questions.prompt: How long have Ben and Lily practised together?
questions.explanation: Ben says they have practised together for three years.

mission.setup: Smarty wants to know how long you have had a hobby or known a friend.

turns.smarty: How long have you studied music?
accept: ^i have studied music (?:since i was a child|all my life|for ages)$
turns.example: I have studied music for three years.
turns.hint: Answer with for three years or since I was a child.

turns.smarty: Have you tried any new hobby recently?
turns.example: Yes, I have started painting recently.
turns.hint: Use recently or lately in your answer.

exposure.gloss: a period of ten years
the time when you were a child
the part of a town near your home

lessons.title: Review
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Ana review friend phrases and life experiences at the café.

practice.prompt: Ana moved away and stopped calling her old classmate. They ***.
practice.explanation: Lost touch means stopped speaking or writing to a friend.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence.
practice.text: Smarty has loved fish ___ he was a kitten.
practice.explanation: Use since before a starting point in the past.

practice.prompt: Match the phrases from Lessons 1–3.
practice.explanation: Each beginning pairs naturally with its ending.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence.
practice.answer: I have been to four museums so far.
practice.explanation: So far shows the total up to now.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: We have a lot in common and hang out every Friday.
practice.answer: We have a lot in common and hang out every Friday.
options: We have a lot in common and hang out every Friday.
We lost touch and never hang out.
We have been to France once or twice.
practice.explanation: Have a lot in common and hang out describe close friends.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud.
practice.text: We have been best friends for three years.
practice.answer: We have been best friends for three years.
practice.explanation: Use for three years for a period of time.

story.hook: What special day are Ana and Leo celebrating at the café?

image.describe: Smarty the black cat sitting at a café table with Ana and Leo, who have a small cake with a candle.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Have you ever visited this café before, Ana?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: Yes, I have been to this café once or twice! Leo is my favourite companion here.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Today is our friendship anniversary! We got to know each other for three years ago, and we have never lost touch.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: We have a lot in common, and we have hung out every weekend since I was a student.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Congratulations! Have a wonderful day!

questions.prompt: Has Ana visited the café before?
questions.explanation: Ana says she has been to this café once or twice.

questions.prompt: How often do Ana and Leo hang out?
questions.explanation: Ana says they have hung out every weekend.

mission.setup: Tell Smarty about a place you have visited and a friend you hang out with.

turns.smarty: Which place have you been to that you really liked?
accept: ^i have been to (?:the sea|the mountains|a forest)$
turns.example: I have been to the museum.
turns.hint: Say I have been to... and name a place.

turns.smarty: How long have you known your friend?
accept: ^i have known (?:him|her|my friend) (?:for three years|for ages|since i was a child|all my life)$
^(?:for three years|for ages|since i was a child)$
turns.example: I have known my friend for ages.
turns.hint: Answer with for ages, for three years, or since I was a child.

exposure.gloss: a friend who spends time or travels with you
a special date you celebrate every year

lessons.title: At the café
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Leo order drinks and snacks at the busy café.

items.example: I would like a hot latte, please.
items.note: A 'latte' is a warm coffee drink made with lots of steamed milk.

image.describe: a warm ceramic cup of latte with foamy milk art on a wooden saucer

items.example: This fresh croissant is delicious for breakfast.
items.note: A 'croissant' is a flaky, curved French pastry often eaten in the morning.

image.describe: a golden flaky crescent-shaped croissant on a small white plate

items.example: Two lattes to take away, please.
items.note: Say 'to take away' when you want to carry your food or drink outside the café.

items.example: Excuse me, is this seat taken?
items.note: Ask 'Is this seat taken?' politely before sitting at an empty chair near someone.

items.example: You paid last time, so it is my round today.
items.note: Say 'My round' when it is your turn to buy drinks for everyone at the table.

items.example: Excuse me, could we have the bill please?
items.note: Say 'the bill please' when you are ready to pay at the end of your visit.

practice.prompt: Look at the picture of a warm drink with foamy milk. Which word fits?
practice.explanation: A latte is a hot drink with lots of warm milk.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: Can I have a croissant to take away?
practice.answer: Can I have a croissant to take away?
options: Can I have a croissant to take away?
Could I have the bill please?
practice.explanation: To take away means you will eat or drink it outside.

practice.prompt: Match each café phrase with when you say it.

pairs.right: When it is your turn to pay for drinks

practice.explanation: These three phrases help you sit, treat friends, and pay in a café.

practice.prompt: Build the polite question.
practice.explanation: Ask Is this seat taken? before sitting down.

practice.prompt: Leo bought the drinks yesterday. Complete what Smarty says.
practice.text: Put your wallet away! It is ___.
practice.explanation: My round means it is your turn to buy the drinks.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud.
practice.text: Excuse me, could I have the bill please?
practice.answer: Excuse me, could I have the bill please?
practice.explanation: Polite way to ask to pay at a café.

practice.prompt: You want to order a drink politely. Which words start your sentence?
practice.explanation: Use Can I have a latte, please? to order.

story.hook: Who pays for the lattes and croissants at the café?

image.describe: Smarty the black cat and Leo at a busy café counter with lattes and croissants on a tray.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Look at the menu board! The barista makes great drinks here.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: I would like a latte and a warm croissant, please. Sit here, or to take away?

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Let us sit here. My round! I will pay for both of us.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Thank you! Look, there is a table by the window. Excuse me, is this seat taken?

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: No, sit down! Enjoy your pastry!

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: That was delicious. Excuse me, the bill please!

questions.prompt: What does Smarty order at the café?
questions.explanation: Smarty orders a latte and a warm croissant.

questions.prompt: What does Smarty ask Mia before sitting down?
questions.explanation: Smarty asks Mia: Is this seat taken?

mission.setup: You are ordering with Smarty at the café.

turns.smarty: I am ordering now. What would you like from the café?
accept: ^(?:can i have|i would like) a (?:latte|croissant)(?: to take away)?(?: please)?$
turns.example: Can I have a latte, please?
turns.hint: Ask for a latte or a croissant.

turns.smarty: We are finished! How do we ask to pay?
accept: ^(?:excuse me )?(?:could i have |can i have )?the bill please$
turns.example: Excuse me, the bill please.
turns.hint: Say The bill please or My round.

exposure.gloss: a big board on the wall showing food and prices
a person who makes coffee drinks in a café
a baked sweet or savoury snack like a croissant

lessons.title: Catching up
lessons.scenario: Zara and Tom bump into each other at the café after a long time.

items.text: What have you been up to?
forms: What has he been up to?
What has she been up to?
items.example: Hi Tom! What have you been up to?
items.note: Ask 'What have you been up to?' when you meet a friend and want to hear their recent news.

items.example: Guess what! I won first prize!
items.note: Say 'Guess what!' right before you share exciting or surprising news.

items.example: I have just heard that Mia got a new job.
items.note: Use 'I have just heard' to tell someone news you learned a moment ago.

items.example: You will never believe who I saw at the station!
items.note: Say 'You will never believe…' before telling a very surprising story.

items.example: Hello Zara, long time no see!
items.note: Say 'long time no see' when you meet a friend you have not seen for weeks or months.

items.example: Sit down and have a tea. Any news?
items.note: Ask 'Any news?' as a quick, friendly way to ask what is new in someone's life.

practice.prompt: You see an old friend after six months. What do you say?
practice.explanation: Long time no see is a friendly greeting after a long time apart.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: What have you been up to lately?
practice.answer: What have you been up to lately?
options: What have you been up to lately?
practice.explanation: What have you been up to? asks about recent activities and news.

practice.prompt: Match each phrase with its purpose.

pairs.right: Telling news you learned moments ago

practice.explanation: Each phrase introduces or asks for news in conversation.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence.
practice.explanation: You will never believe introduces a big surprise.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence.
practice.text: ___ that Omar passed his driving test!
practice.explanation: Use I have just heard to share fresh news.

practice.prompt: Say the greeting aloud.
practice.text: Long time no see! Any news?
practice.answer: Long time no see! Any news?
practice.explanation: Natural way to greet a friend and ask for updates.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence about something that happened moments ago.
practice.text: ___ arrived at the café!
practice.explanation: Use I have just for an action finished a moment ago.

tell news clearly to a group of people
surprise someone very much

lessons.title: Personality
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Mia describe their friends' personalities over tea.

items.example: Leo was shy at first, but now he loves to sing.
items.note: Someone who is 'shy' feels quiet or nervous when meeting new people.

image.describe: a cute small cat peeking shyly from behind a big menu card at a café table

items.example: Ana is generous and always shares her snacks.
items.note: A 'generous' person likes to give time, help, or presents to others.

items.example: Sam is reliable and always arrives on time.
items.note: Someone who is 'reliable' does what they promise and can be trusted.

items.example: My brother is stubborn and never changes his mind.
items.note: A 'stubborn' person refuses to change their plan or idea even when others ask.

items.example: Zara is easy-going and never gets angry.
items.note: Someone who is 'easy-going' is relaxed and happy with almost any plan.

items.example: Smarty has a great sense of humour and makes us laugh.
items.note: Someone with a good 'sense of humour' enjoys jokes and makes other people smile.

practice.prompt: Look at the picture of the cat hiding behind the menu. Which word fits?
practice.explanation: Shy describes someone who feels nervous or quiet around new people.

practice.prompt: Match each personality word with its meaning.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence.
practice.text: Ben is very ___ and never worries about small problems.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence.
practice.answer: Mia has a great sense of humour.

having good manners and speaking kindly
liking to talk a lot

lessons.title: If we miss it
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Omar are hurrying to catch a connecting train and making backup plans.

items.text: If we miss it we will
forms: if we miss it we will
items.example: If we miss it we will take the next train.
items.note: Use 'If we miss it we will' to explain your backup plan if you are late for a train.

items.example: We will be late unless we run now.
items.note: Use 'unless' to mean 'if not'—for example, 'unless we run' means 'if we do not run'.

items.example: I will text you as soon as we get to the hotel.
items.note: Say 'as soon as' for the exact moment one thing finishes and the next thing starts.

items.example: Take a warm coat in case it gets cold.
items.note: Say 'in case' when you prepare something now for a possible problem later.

items.example: We will catch the train as long as it is on time.
items.note: Say 'as long as' to mean 'only if' this one condition happens.

items.example: I will take it if there is a window seat.
items.note: Use 'I will take it if' when you agree to a ticket or seat on one condition.

grammar.title: First conditional and time words
grammar.explanation: After 'if', 'unless', 'as soon as', 'in case', and 'as long as', use the present simple tense—never 'will'. Put 'will' in the other part of the sentence for the future result.
examples: If we miss it we will wait at the café.
I will call you as soon as the train stops.

grammar.title: Past perfect: had + past participle
grammar.explanation: Use 'had' plus a past participle for the earlier of two past actions, and the past simple for the later action. Words like 'already', 'never', 'by the time', 'after', and 'before' make the order clear.
examples: I had already bought the tickets before we arrived.
She had never seen an ancient coin.
By the time we arrived, the visit had not yet started.

lessons.title: Gerund or infinitive

items.example: I enjoy doing origami in the evening.

items.note: Always use 'to' plus the base verb after 'want'.

items.note: Say 'give up' plus a noun or -ing verb when you stop trying or quit an activity.

grammar.title: Gerund (-ing) or infinitive (to + verb)
grammar.explanation: After 'enjoy', 'give up', and 'keep on', use the -ing form of the next verb. After 'want', 'manage', and 'would like', use 'to' plus the base verb.

I would like to learn sewing, and I want to make a bag.

lessons.title: Telling a story
lessons.canDo: Use past perfect in a story
lessons.scenario: Smarty tells a dramatic mystery story in the newsroom.

items.example: Long ago there lived a clever inventor in a quiet mountain village.
items.note: Start a classic tale or history story with 'Long ago there lived...' to set the scene.

items.example: Our boots were dirty because it had been raining all morning.
items.note: Use 'it had been raining' (past perfect continuous) for rain that continued up to a past moment.

items.example: We reached the station at nine, but by then the last train had left.
items.note: Say 'by then' to mean 'at or before that point in the story'.

items.example: He opened the old box, and what he did not know was that a map was inside.
items.note: Use 'what he did not know' to build mystery when a character misses an important secret.

items.example: Leo found a key that someone had dropped a few days earlier.
items.note: Use 'a few days earlier' with the past perfect to jump back to an earlier event.

items.example: As soon as he had read the letter, he ran to the newsroom.
items.note: Use 'as soon as he had' + past participle to show one action finished right before the next.

grammar.title: Past perfect in narration
grammar.explanation: When telling a story in the past, use the past perfect (had + past participle) for an action that happened before another past action. Use had been + -ing (it had been raining) for a background action that continued up to that moment.
examples: By then, everyone had gone home.
The street was cold because it had been raining.

lessons.title: Opinions in the media

grammar.title: Past ability and possibility
grammar.explanation: For one difficult success in the past, use 'was able to', 'managed to', or 'succeeded in' + -ing (do not use 'could' for a single hard achievement). For past inability, use 'was unable to' or 'were not able to'. For possibility, use 'might'.
examples: I managed to climb the steep path.
We succeeded in crossing the cold river.
We were not able to see the summit in the clouds.

grammar.title: so vs. such

lessons.title: He must be
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Ana find clues backstage at the theatre and guess who left them.

items.example: Leo is smiling, so he must be in a good mood.
items.note: Use 'must be' when you are almost sure something is true right now.

items.example: Mia is quiet, so she might be nervous.
items.note: Say 'might be' when something is possible, but you are not sure.

items.example: It can not be Leo's hat because his hat is blue.
items.note: Use 'can not be' when you are almost sure something is impossible.

items.example: The lights are on, so they may be on stage.
items.note: Say 'may be' to make a polite, possible guess about now.

items.example: Whose scarf is this? It could be Zara's.
items.note: Use 'could be' when there is a chance something is true.

items.example: Snow in July? You must be joking!
items.note: Say 'You must be joking' when someone says something surprising or hard to believe.

grammar.title: Guessing about now: must, might, may, could, can not
grammar.explanation: Use 'must be' when clues make you 95% sure. Use 'might be', 'may be', or 'could be' when something is possible (about 50% sure). Use 'can not be' when you are 95% sure it is impossible.
examples: He has been working all day, so he must be tired.
She is not here yet; she might be on the bus.
It can not be midnight—the sun is still out!

practice.prompt: Ben ran all the way to the theatre and has no water. How sure are you that he is thirsty?
practice.explanation: Running without water is a strong clue, so use 'He must be'.

practice.prompt: Listen and choose the sentence you hear.

practice.answer: It can not be Ben because he is at home.
options: It can not be Ben because he is at home.
It must be Ben because he is at home.
It could be Ben because he is at home.
practice.explanation: If Ben is at home, it is impossible for him to be here, so use 'It can not be'.

practice.prompt: Match each phrase with how sure you are.
practice.explanation: Must be = sure yes, might be = possible, can not be = sure no, you must be joking = disbelief.

practice.prompt: Zara is not in the room. Maybe she is in the café. Complete the sentence.

practice.explanation: When something is possible, use 'She might be'.

practice.explanation: For two people when something is possible, use 'They may be'.

practice.prompt: Build a guess about the red scarf on the table.
practice.explanation: 'It could be' shows a possible guess.

practice.prompt: Sam says he ate ten pizzas for lunch! What do you say?
practice.explanation: Say 'You must be joking!' when someone says something hard to believe.

lessons.scenario: Ben fell out with Tom before rehearsal and asks Smarty and Mia for advice.

items.example: You should try speaking to Tom after rehearsal.

items.example: Why do not you send him a nice message?
items.note: Use 'Why do not you...' to suggest an easy idea.

items.example: It might help to say sorry first.
items.note: Say 'It might help to...' when you want to give gentle advice.

grammar.title: Patterns for giving advice
grammar.explanation: Notice what comes after each phrase: 'Why do not you' and 'It might help to' take the base verb (go, call, say). 'Have you thought about' takes a noun or -ing verb (writing, speaking). 'You should try' can take -ing or to + verb.
examples: Why do not you call him?
It might help to take a rest.
Have you thought about practising together?

practice.prompt: You have a problem and want Smarty's advice. What do you ask?

practice.explanation: 'If I were in your shoes' means 'If I were in your situation'.

lines.speaker: Smarty

questions.prompt: What kind of film does Mia want to watch?

An action film is the worst.

questions.prompt: How does Lily start her opinion?
questions.explanation: Lily says: Personally I think an action film is more exciting.

mission.setup: Smarty asks for your opinion in the club-room. Answer in your own words.

turns.smarty: We want to watch a film this evening. What do you think?
accept: ^(?:as i see it|personally i think|from my point of view|i feel that|i strongly believe|it seems to me that) (?:a comedy|a cartoon|an action film|a documentary|a horror film) is (?:great|interesting|exciting|better|the best|boring)$

turns.hint: Start with Personally I think or As I see it, then name a film type.

turns.smarty: What about our town park? Should we clean up the litter there?
accept: ^(?:i strongly believe|i feel that|it seems to me that|as i see it|personally i think|from my point of view) (?:we should|everyone should|we must) (?:clean|help|recycle)(?: the park| up the litter| more)?$
turns.example: I strongly believe we should clean the park.
turns.hint: Use I strongly believe or I feel that and say what we should do.

lessons.title: Question tags
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Mia double-check details for the weekend picnic in the club-room.

items.example: It is a sunny day, is not it?
items.note: Add 'is not it?' at the end of a positive 'it is' sentence to check if the listener agrees.

items.example: You like chocolate cake, do not you?
items.note: Use 'do not you?' after a positive 'you' statement to confirm what you think is true.

items.example: Ben did not miss the bus, did he?
items.note: Add 'did he?' after a negative past statement about a boy or man to check the fact.

items.example: They have already bought the tickets, have not they?
items.note: Use 'have not they?' after a positive 'they have' statement to double-check.

items.example: I am on the team, am I not?
items.note: Add 'am I not?' after 'I am' when you want someone to confirm something about you.

items.example: You will not forget the camera, will you?
items.note: Use 'will you?' after 'you will not' to make sure someone remembers a promise.

grammar.title: How question tags work
grammar.explanation: A positive statement takes a negative tag, and a negative statement takes a positive tag. Match the helper verb (is, do, did, have, will) and the subject pronoun.
examples: It is cold outside, is not it?
He did not call yesterday, did he?

practice.prompt: Complete the question tag for a positive 'It is' sentence.
practice.text: It is a great idea, ___
practice.explanation: It is takes the negative tag is not it?.

practice.prompt: You think Mia likes tea. Check with her.
practice.text: You like hot tea, ___
practice.explanation: A positive present simple statement with you takes do not you?.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: Ben did not miss the bus, did he?
practice.answer: Ben did not miss the bus, did he?
options: Ben did not miss the bus, did he?
Ben missed the bus, did he?
Ben did not miss the bus, will you?
practice.explanation: Because did not miss is negative, the tag is positive: did he?.

practice.prompt: Match the start of each sentence with its question tag.
practice.explanation: Match the verb and subject: have -> have not they?, I am -> am I not?, will not -> will you?.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence to check if Sam and Leo have the snacks.
practice.answer: They have got the snacks, have not they?
practice.explanation: They have takes have not they? at the end.

practice.prompt: Check that you are right. Complete the question.
practice.text: I am right about the time, ___
practice.explanation: After I am, use am I not? to ask for confirmation.

practice.prompt: Remind Sam not to forget the map. Complete the question.
practice.text: You will not forget the map, ___
practice.explanation: You will not takes the positive tag will you?.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud. You can try again.
practice.text: It is a sunny day, is not it?
practice.answer: It is a sunny day, is not it?
practice.explanation: Let your voice rise at the end on is not it? when checking information.

story.hook: Did Ben remember the picnic basket?

image.describe: Smarty and Mia stand by the club-room table checking a picnic list while Sam looks out the window waiting for Ben.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: We are ready for our picnic in the park. Let us double-check everything.

questions.explanation: Mia says: It is a warm, sunny morning, is not it?.

questions.prompt: What did Sam ask about Ben?
questions.explanation: Sam asks: Ben did not forget the blanket, did he?.

questions.prompt: What does Smarty remind Mia to do?
questions.explanation: Smarty says: You will not forget to close the window, will you?.

mission.setup: Smarty wants to check some facts with you using question tags.

turns.smarty: Look outside! Tell me it is a nice day and check if I agree.
accept: ^it is a (?:nice|sunny|warm|great|beautiful) day is not it$
turns.example: It is a sunny day, is not it?
turns.hint: Say It is a sunny day, is not it?

turns.hint: Say You like fish, do not you?

accept: ^you will not forget your umbrella will you$

turns.hint: Say You will not forget your umbrella, will you?

exposure.gloss: to check that something is true
to check something a second time
a short question added to the end of a sentence
to repeat the verb from the first part of a sentence

lessons.title: Giving reasons
lessons.scenario: Leo arrives late to the club-room and explains why everyone is delayed.

items.example: I am late, and the reason is that my bus was delayed.
items.note: Say 'the reason is' right before you explain why something happened.

items.example: It was raining hard, and that is why we stayed inside.
items.note: Use 'that is why' after giving a cause to show its result.

items.example: We missed the train because of the traffic jam.
items.note: Put 'because of' before a noun or thing that caused a problem or result.

items.example: The game was cancelled due to the storm.
items.note: Use 'due to' before a noun to give a clear, slightly formal reason.

items.example: Owing to the snow, the school was closed yesterday.
items.note: Say 'owing to' before a noun, often at the start of a sentence, to explain a cause.

items.example: The bridge is broken. For this reason, we must go by boat.
items.note: Start a new sentence with 'For this reason,' to connect a fact to your next action.

grammar.title: Noun after because of, due to, owing to
grammar.explanation: Follow because of, due to, and owing to with a noun phrase like the rain or the traffic jam. Follow the reason is, that is why, and for this reason with a full clause.
examples: We stayed home because of the rain.
It rained. For this reason, we stayed home.

practice.prompt: A noun phrase follows the blank. Choose the right phrase.
practice.text: We were late ___ the traffic jam.
practice.explanation: Use because of before a noun like the traffic jam.

practice.prompt: The first part gives the cause. Connect it to the result.
practice.text: There was a power cut, and ___ the computer is off.
practice.explanation: That is why links a cause to its result clause.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: The game was cancelled due to the storm.
practice.answer: The game was cancelled due to the storm.
options: The game was cancelled due to the storm.
The train was delayed due to the snow.
The game was cancelled because of the rain.
practice.explanation: Listen for cancelled due to the storm.

practice.prompt: Match the two parts of each sentence.

pairs.left: I am tired, and the reason is
The park is closed. For this reason,

practice.explanation: Owing to takes a noun; the reason is and For this reason take full clauses.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence explaining why you are late.
practice.answer: The reason is that my bus was delayed.
practice.explanation: Start with The reason is that, followed by my bus was delayed.

practice.prompt: Start the sentence with a formal reason before the noun.
practice.text: ___ the snow, the station was closed.
practice.explanation: Owing to goes right before a noun phrase like the snow.

practice.prompt: Connect the first sentence to the action in the second sentence.
practice.text: The tap is broken. ___, there is no water.
practice.explanation: For this reason introduces a whole result sentence.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud. You can try again.
practice.text: We missed the train because of the traffic jam.
practice.answer: We missed the train because of the traffic jam.
practice.explanation: Use because of smoothly before the noun phrase the traffic jam.

story.hook: Why did Leo arrive wet and late to the club-room?

image.describe: Leo stands in the club-room doorway holding a wet umbrella while Smarty and Ana look at the rain outside the window.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Hello, Leo! You are very wet and twenty minutes late.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Sorry! I am late, and the reason is that my bus stopped near the bridge.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: Was there a traffic jam?

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Yes, there was a big traffic jam because of the thunderstorm.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: And the train was cancelled due to the lightning, was it?

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Right! Owing to the storm, no trains were running. That is why I walked.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: What a cause and effect! For this reason, let us make hot tea for Leo.

questions.prompt: Why was there a big traffic jam?
questions.explanation: Leo says: there was a big traffic jam because of the thunderstorm.

questions.prompt: Why were no trains running?
questions.explanation: Leo says: Owing to the storm, no trains were running.

questions.prompt: What does Ana suggest at the end?
questions.explanation: Ana says: For this reason, let us make hot tea for Leo.

mission.setup: Smarty asks why you were late to the meeting. Give clear reasons.

turns.smarty: You arrived late today! Why did that happen?
accept: ^(?:i am late because of|it happened because of|i was late because of|it was due to) the (?:rain|snow|storm|traffic jam|thunderstorm)$
^the reason is that (?:it was raining|my bus was delayed|i missed the bus)$
turns.example: I was late because of the traffic jam.
turns.hint: Use because of the rain/traffic jam or the reason is that...

turns.smarty: Oh no! What did you do next?
accept: ^that is why i (?:walked|came by bus|came by car|took a taxi)$
^for this reason i (?:walked|came by bus|came by car|took a taxi)$
turns.example: That is why I walked.
turns.hint: Start with That is why I... or For this reason I...

exposure.gloss: the reason you give to make something clear
something that makes another thing happen
a change that happens because of something
what happens at the end because of a cause

lessons.title: Review
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Zara share opinions about town litter, check facts, and explain reasons in the club-room.

practice.prompt: Choose the phrase that introduces your personal view.
practice.explanation: From my point of view shows how you see an issue.

practice.prompt: Check that Zara and Tom have cleaned the park.
practice.text: They have cleaned the park, ___
practice.explanation: They have takes the negative tag have not they?.

practice.prompt: Give a reason before the noun phrase 'air pollution'.
practice.text: Many people are ill ___ air pollution.
practice.explanation: Use due to before a noun phrase like air pollution.

practice.prompt: Match the phrases with their roles in a discussion.
practice.explanation: As I see it shares a view, is not it? checks agreement, and For this reason connects a cause to an action.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence giving a gentle opinion.
practice.answer: It seems to me that litter is a problem.
practice.explanation: It seems to me that introduces a polite, clear opinion.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: You care about nature, do not you?
practice.answer: You care about nature, do not you?
options: You care about nature, do not you?
You care about music, do not you?
They care about nature, have not they?
practice.explanation: You with a positive verb takes do not you?.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud. You can try again.
practice.text: I strongly believe we can solve this problem.
practice.answer: I strongly believe we can solve this problem.
practice.explanation: Practise combining I strongly believe with a clear action.

story.hook: Why is there so much litter near the river?

image.describe: Smarty, Zara, and Tom sit around a table in the club-room looking at a town map with green pins along the river.

lines.speaker: Zara
lines.text: As I see it, the park near the river is very dirty this week.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: It is full of rubbish, is not it? The reason is that there were many visitors yesterday.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: And there are not enough rubbish bins because of the festival, are there?

lines.speaker: Zara
lines.text: Right! Owing to many people, the bins were full early. That is why litter is on the grass.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: You want to help clean it up tomorrow, do not you?

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: I strongly believe we should! For this reason, let us meet at nine o'clock.

questions.prompt: What is Zara's opinion about the park?
questions.answer: It is very dirty this week.
options: It is very dirty this week.
It is closed due to snow.
questions.explanation: Zara says: As I see it, the park near the river is very dirty this week.

questions.prompt: Why were the bins full early?
questions.explanation: Zara says: Owing to many people, the bins were full early.

mission.setup: Smarty asks you to share your opinion, check a fact, and give a reason.

turns.smarty: What is your opinion on riding a bicycle to school?
accept: ^(?:as i see it|personally i think|from my point of view|i strongly believe|i feel that) (?:riding a bicycle|a bicycle) is (?:healthy|cheap|great|better|fast|good)$
turns.example: Personally I think a bicycle is healthy.
turns.hint: Use Personally I think or As I see it and describe riding a bicycle.

turns.smarty: Why is a bicycle better than a car in town?
accept: ^(?:the reason is that )?(?:there is no traffic jam|it is cheap|it is healthy)$
^(?:it is good )?because of (?:the traffic jam|air pollution)$
turns.example: It is good because of the traffic jam.
turns.hint: Give a reason with the reason is or because of.

lessons.title: Linking ideas
lessons.scenario: Ana and Tom compare two ideas for the club-room weekend activity.

items.example: The jacket is expensive. However, it is very warm.
items.note: Start a new sentence with 'However,' to introduce a fact that contrasts with your first point.

items.example: Although it was raining, we walked to the park.
items.note: Use 'although' before a full clause to show a surprising contrast between two facts.

items.example: In spite of the cold weather, we played football outside.
items.note: Put 'in spite of' before a noun to show that something happened anyway.

items.example: Even though I was tired, I helped my friend.
items.note: Use 'even though' for a strong contrast, just like 'although' but with extra emphasis.

items.example: Living in town is noisy. On the other hand, everything is near.
items.note: Say 'On the other hand,' when you move to the opposite side of an argument.

items.example: Mia enjoys skiing, whereas Sam prefers swimming.
items.note: Use 'whereas' in the middle of a sentence to compare two opposite facts.

grammar.title: Contrasting clauses vs. nouns
grammar.explanation: Use although, even though, and whereas with a subject and verb. Use in spite of with a noun. Use However and On the other hand at the start of a new sentence.
examples: Although he was ill, he came.
In spite of his cold, he came.

practice.prompt: A noun phrase follows the blank. Choose the right linking phrase.
practice.text: ___ the rain, we had a great picnic.
practice.explanation: In spite of goes before a noun like the rain, while although and even though take a verb.

practice.prompt: Compare Mia and Sam's hobbies in one sentence.
practice.text: Mia likes painting, ___ Sam prefers woodwork.
practice.explanation: Use whereas in the middle of a sentence to contrast two people or things.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: The camera is small. However, it takes amazing photos.
practice.answer: The camera is small. However, it takes amazing photos.
options: The camera is small. However, it takes amazing photos.
The camera is big. However, it is very cheap.
Although the camera is small, it is broken.
practice.explanation: However starts the second sentence to show a positive contrast.

practice.prompt: Match the two halves of each contrasting sentence.

pairs.left: The hotel is cheap. On the other hand,
pairs.right: it is far from the station.

pairs.left: Even though the exam was difficult,

practice.explanation: Match the contrasting ideas logically.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence showing a contrast about the weather.
practice.answer: Although it was cold we went outside.
practice.explanation: Although introduces the clause it was cold before the main clause.

practice.prompt: Add strong emphasis to the contrast. Complete the sentence.
practice.text: ___ he was nervous, Omar spoke clearly on stage.
practice.explanation: Even though goes before a full clause like he was nervous.

practice.prompt: Introduce the opposite side of the argument.
practice.text: Summer is hot. ___, we can swim in the sea.
practice.explanation: On the other hand opens a new sentence with the other side of the topic.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud. You can try again.
practice.text: Mia enjoys skiing, whereas Sam prefers swimming.
practice.answer: Mia enjoys skiing, whereas Sam prefers swimming.
practice.explanation: Pause lightly before whereas when comparing two people.

story.hook: Can Ana and Tom agree on a weekend trip?

image.describe: Ana and Tom sit at the club-room table comparing a mountain trail map and a museum leaflet while Smarty listens carefully.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: I want to hike in the forest tomorrow. However, the forecast says it may rain.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Although the forest is beautiful, a wet trail is dangerous.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: True! On the other hand, the nature reserve is quiet in the rain.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: You love walking outside, whereas I prefer staying dry in the museum.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: What a clear contrast! Even though you want different things, your ideas even out.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: In spite of the cloudy sky, we can visit the museum first and walk if the sun comes out.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Despite my fear of rain, that sounds like a great compromise!

questions.prompt: Why is Tom worried about hiking in the forest?
questions.answer: The trail is dangerous in the rain.
options: The trail is dangerous in the rain.
questions.explanation: Tom says: Although the forest is beautiful, a wet trail is dangerous.

questions.prompt: How does Tom compare himself and Ana?
questions.answer: Ana loves walking outside, whereas Tom prefers the museum.
options: Ana loves walking outside, whereas Tom prefers the museum.
Ana prefers the museum, whereas Tom loves the forest.
questions.explanation: Tom says: You love walking outside, whereas I prefer staying dry in the museum.

mission.setup: Smarty gives you one side of a topic. Add a contrasting idea!

turns.smarty: Our room is quite small. Can you add a positive contrast with However or On the other hand?
accept: ^(?:however|on the other hand) (?:it is|our room is) (?:warm|clean|nice|cozy|great|near|quiet)$
turns.example: However, it is clean.
turns.hint: Start with However or On the other hand, then say something good about the room.

turns.smarty: Compare tea and coffee using whereas.

exposure.gloss: a clear difference between two things
to become balanced or equal
without being stopped by something
in spite of what was just said

lessons.title: Adding points
lessons.scenario: Smarty helps Lily organize her points for a community charity proposal.

items.example: We need drinking water as well as snacks for the trip.
items.note: Use 'as well as' to add one more thing or idea onto something you just mentioned.

items.example: The hotel has a swimming pool. In addition, breakfast is free.
items.note: Start a sentence with 'In addition,' to give an extra supporting point.

items.example: First of all, let us check the agenda.
items.note: Say 'First of all,' to introduce the very first point in a list or discussion.

items.example: Lastly, we must clean the room before we leave.
items.note: Use 'Lastly,' right before your final point so listeners know you are finishing.

items.example: The solar panel saves money. What is more, it is clean.
items.note: Say 'What is more,' when your next point is even stronger or more exciting.

items.example: To begin with, I would like to thank everyone for coming.
items.note: Use 'To begin with,' to open your explanation with your first main idea.

grammar.title: Ordering your points clearly
grammar.explanation: Open with First of all or To begin with. Add extra points with In addition, What is more, or as well as. Close your list with Lastly.
examples: To begin with, the park is dirty. In addition, there is litter near the lake. Lastly, we can clean it together.

practice.prompt: Start the meeting with the very first point.
practice.text: ___, let us look at today's agenda.
practice.explanation: First of all introduces your opening point.

practice.prompt: Add fruit to the shopping list.
practice.text: We bought bread and cheese ___ fresh fruit.
practice.explanation: Use as well as to join an extra noun onto a list.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: The solar panel saves money. What is more, it is clean.
practice.answer: The solar panel saves money. What is more, it is clean.
options: The solar panel saves money. What is more, it is clean.
The solar panel is cheap. Lastly, it is small.
To begin with, the solar panel saves electricity.
practice.explanation: What is more introduces an even stronger second point.

practice.prompt: Match each phrase with its place in a talk.
practice.explanation: To begin with opens, In addition adds, and Lastly finishes.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence adding an extra benefit.
practice.answer: In addition the workshop is free.
practice.explanation: In addition starts the sentence to add another positive fact.

practice.prompt: Open Lily's proposal with her first point.
practice.text: ___, we want to raise money for the library.
practice.explanation: To begin with introduces the very first point of a talk.

practice.prompt: Finish the list with the final action.
practice.text: ___, we will share the photos online.
practice.explanation: Lastly signals that this is the final point.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud. You can try again.
practice.text: First of all, we need a clear agenda.
practice.answer: First of all, we need a clear agenda.
practice.explanation: Use First of all to organize your ideas from the start.

exposure.gloss: a set of items or points in order
the order in which things happen or are said
in addition to what was just said

lessons.title: Disagreeing nicely
lessons.scenario: Omar and Mia disagree politely about buying a big screen for the club-room.

items.example: I see your point, but the screen is too expensive.
items.note: Say 'I see your point, but...' to show you understand the other person before sharing a different view.

items.example: I am afraid I disagree with that proposal.
items.note: Use 'I am afraid I disagree' to say no politely without sounding angry.

items.example: I am not convinced that this is the best solution.
items.note: Say 'I am not convinced' when someone's reason has not persuaded you yet.

items.example: That may be true, but we do not have enough money.
items.note: Use 'That may be true, but...' to accept a fact while showing a bigger problem.

items.example: We both have strong views, so let us agree to differ.
items.note: Say 'Let us agree to differ' to end a friendly debate peacefully when neither side changes.

items.example: I take your point about the price, so let us look for a discount.
items.note: Say 'I take your point' to admit that the other speaker made a good argument.

grammar.title: Softening disagreement
grammar.explanation: Soften disagreement by starting with I am afraid or I am not convinced, or by accepting part of the idea first with I see your point, but... or That may be true, but...
examples: I see your point, but I am not convinced.
I am afraid I disagree.

practice.prompt: Which phrase is the most polite way to disagree in a meeting?

practice.prompt: Show you understand Omar's idea before giving a problem.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.

options: I am not convinced that this is the best solution.
I am convinced that this is a great idea.
I am afraid I disagree with your solution.
practice.explanation: Listen for the negative: I am not convinced.

practice.prompt: Match each polite phrase with what it does.

pairs.right: admits the other person made a good point

lessons.title: Pros and cons

items.example: Every proposal has a drawback, so we must check carefully.

items.example: Clean air is a benefit for everyone in town.

lessons.title: Choosing
lessons.scenario: Smarty and his friends choose between a forest picnic and a museum visit.

items.example: Shall we go for the picnic in the park?

items.example: I would prefer to visit the museum because it is cloudy.

items.note: Ask 'How about...?' followed by a noun or -ing verb to make a friendly suggestion.

lessons.title: Summing up

items.example: To sum up, we have a clear solution.
items.note: Start with 'To sum up,' when you are about to give a short summary of the whole discussion.

items.example: In conclusion, the proposal is a great benefit for our town.
items.note: Use 'In conclusion,' at the end of a talk or report to state your final point.

items.example: All in all, it was a great meeting.

items.note: Use 'The main point is...' to remind everyone of the single most important idea.

items.example: Looking back, it was worth it.
